utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Just a word of welcome to everybody from the recess. I hope everybody is well-rested and all ready to move on with the case without much delay. Before we start, I have a few remarks to make. And I'll be addressing myself mainly to the Defence team, Mr. Milovancevic, if you can be listening to what I'm going to be saying. When we parted, Mr. Milovancevic, the Defence had undertaken to file documents by Monday, the 17th of July. And these were not filed until 1.00 on the 19th of July without any reasons being provided for the delay. That's the one point that I have to complain about. And apparently the list that was provided on that day instead of having ten witnesses it had only eight witnesses, the majority of whom were not in the original ten that had been supplied to the Prosecution as the starting witnesses of the Defence. Are you able to update the Court as to what has happened from that point and what the position is right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Your Honour has said is correct. After departing from the Tribunal for Belgrade, the Defence team contacted the witnesses. The changes in the names of the witness list occurred due to the physical impossibility of contacting witnesses who are away on holiday. This was a big problem for the Defence team and we did our utmost to contact those witnesses we could in order to continue with the trial. Of course, we were very unhappy about this but we had to cope with the situation such as it was. We were unable to contact and prepare the witnesses we had intended to call as the first ten. That is the only reason. We did inform the Chamber of our fears that this might happen. We didn't know, however, that the problems would be as great as they turned out to be. We are, however, ready to continue with our case now. The delay so that the 19th is the date rather than the 17th when the documents were submitted in July is due to the fact that when we arrived in Belgrade, we had many deadlines to meet and we did our very best. The delay is a result of circumstances we could not influence. We did our best to meet all the deadlines but we were late. We tried to explain to our learned friends that this was due to objective reasons and I hope that the Chamber will take this into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing is that you didn't even give the Chamber the courtesy of an explanation with your filings that came late. This is the problem. And the Chamber was now in the dark as to, are you flouting the Chamber's orders or what are you doing? To get an explanation now, when the Chamber is asking for the explanation, is not absolutely appropriate. It would have been better to give your explanations with your late filings or even before the late filings, just to explain why it was difficult for you to meet the deadlines. Thank you any way for your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something, Your Honour? I accept Your Honour's criticism and I understand that we have made an omission. We were doing our best to meet the deadlines but this is no justification and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that apology. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I may, unfortunately the situation is actually much worse than what was described by the Court and I think it's important that it be put on the record. On the 19th of July, Your Honour is correct that the list of ten witnesses was provided. It was ten witnesses that were provided on the 19th of July and that was the list that was supposed to be provided on the 14th of July. So that was five days late. That would have been fine. We could have lived with that. We got to work on the ten witnesses, we have been spending these weeks preparing them. However, on -- one week ago, on the 7th of August, we received a new list and that is the list that I think Your Honour was referring to with eight witnesses. Now if those eight witnesses had been eight of the ten, fine, that would have also been no problem. Unfortunately not the case. Of the eight witnesses only three were from the original list of ten. So -- and this week, the three witnesses -- we then tried to see through Chambers if the list could be somehow reorganised, no, unfortunately that seemed to be impossible so there week the three witnesses who are scheduled to testify are witnesses that we were first notified about one week ago. Which is really disadvantaged the Prosecution, has made it very difficult for us to prepare properly for cross-examination. I find it very hard to believe that the Defence only knew one week ago that this was going to be the list of witnesses that they were going to call and that they didn't know in the 19 days between the 19th of July and the 7th of August that they didn't know that that list had changed in some respect and they never notified us. They could have notified us on a sort of rolling basis about adjustments that were being made to the list. That did not happen. I can see no other reason than to gain strategic advantage and to leave us disadvantaged. I cannot imagine any other reason because they had to have known before last Monday that the list of ten was not going to be their list for the first witnesses. The practical consequence much that, we considered last week seeking a delay in the trial of one week; however, we are aware of the pressures to move forward, we decided not to do that. However, there are -- as I see it -- two potential consequences to this having been done. The first is that we may have exhibits that we will seek to use in cross-examination that are not translated because we did not have time to both identify them and get them translated. The second is that we may seek a short delay after the testimony of one of the witnesses this week of a day, perhaps certainly no more than a day, perhaps if it finishes one day and start the next day, we'll try to avoid that but it's very difficult with this short notice to be completely and fully prepared. So I wanted that to -- the Court to be aware of that and for that to be on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. May I just understand: You're talking of exhibits that may not be translated. Do you get these exhibits in B/C/S and it's your responsibility to translate them or do you get them translated for you by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, these are not exhibits that the Defence is going to use. These are documents that we have identified on our own as being potentially relevant during the cross-examination of the witnesses. And they are at present only in B/C/S and we are endeavouring to get them translated as quickly as possible but they may not be -- it's quite likely that some of them will not be fully translated and we'll have to use them in court in an untranslated form. That can be done, we can show the witness and have the witness read out the relevant portions and they will be translated here in the courtroom but of course it takes more time. It's awkward, it's not optimal for the court or the parties to be using documents which are not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess you have said what you have to say, Mr. Milovancevic, unless you have anything else to respond specifically to what Mr. Whiting has said. If not, I would like to move on. I don't want us to waste more time on these procedural issues. I would like us to get on to the witness as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may proceed with the witness, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, before we do that, I think as a result of the happenings of the last couple of weeks, the Trial Chamber will find it very difficult to extend any courtesies to the Defence in terms of allowing them time for extensions unless the extensions are requested in terms of the Rules and are accompanied by cogent reasons. Mr. Milovancevic, you may call your next witness, sorry, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sorry, I just had a few small matters and they won't take much time. The first is that there are a few other things that have not been complied with that are long overdue. The first is that on the 7th of July the Defence stated that Mr. Martic will testify and that they would provide a 65 ter summary for him along with the other witnesses by the 14th of July. Of course, those 65 ter summaries as we've just been discussing weren't provided until the 19th of July but notably absent was a 65 ter summary for Mr. Martic. We have not to date received that so it's now some four or five weeks overdue and we think that should be provided immediately. We think we are entitled to it. Second point is that of the 53 witnesses for whom we were provided 65 ter summaries, seven of them did not have 65 ter summaries. We have provided this list to the Defence and asked for their 65 ter summaries. The Defence has indicated these witnesses may be dropped from their list. This is something that I think we should be informed about as soon as possible. That leads me into my the next point which is the Defence indicated on the 14th of July that no later than one week before trial they would essentially provide a kind of revised witness list. I think indicating which witnesses might be dropped but also indicating which witnesses would testify pursuant to 92 bis. That has not been done. It was not ordered by the court but it was indicated by the Defence that they would do that. The final thing -- no not the final thing only the next thing is that on the Defence has indicated repeatedly that after we requested it and it was ordered by the Trial Chamber, that they would provide to us all of the exhibits that were referenced during their opening statement but which were not contained on the exhibit list. On the 14th of July, the Defence indicated that some of the exhibits they believed were in fact on their exhibit list though contained within other documents. The Court ordered the Defence to tell the Prosecution by the 17th of July wherein the exhibits those documents were contained and if they were not contained in their exhibits to provide them to us. That has also not been complied with. We were also supposed to get translations of the exhibits that did -- were on their exhibit list. Today we did receive some translation was a note indicating that a number of exhibits are being dropped from the list but no indication as to which ones are being dropped. It seems to us that that also should be provided. Finally in the category of unfulfilled obligations the Defence has been ordered, and this was on the 11th of July, to provide the expert reports and translations by today. I don't know if the Defence is prepared to do that. We have not received them as of yet. Just as final matter while I'm on my feet, we received on Friday a protective measures motion with respect to certain witnesses. I'm prepared to provide an oral response if that suits the Court to that now. Though of course we would have to do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That last point we'll deal with later. Can we first deal with the seven points that you raised apart from that last one of protective measures. Mr. Milovancevic, if I may just sort of lead you on these issues that have been raised by your learned friend, is Mr. Martic going to testify? And if he's going to testify, when we can expect his 65 ter summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have informed the Chamber that Mr. Martic will testify. In the meantime, we were in Belgrade until two days ago to prepare witnesses for the trial, and we were therefore not in contact with Mr. Martic. This is a circumstance making our job more difficult. Within the following week, we shall fully update the Chamber about the situation. Secondly, I have the impression from what my learned friend has said that he feels we are trying to obstruct the work of the OTP. But this is not the case, Your Honour. There are objective problems. The OTP also overstepped some deadlines. For example they were supposed to submit something by the 25th of December 2005 and they were seven days late and submitted it in 2006. In the meantime one of our witnesses has died, others are not available. Some lack passports. They are refugees. And it's very difficult to get them to come here because we have to get them passports and the passports are valid only for a week. So these are the problems we have been dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you, Mr. Milovancevic? We are dealing with Mr. Martic's testimony. Can we deal with that and that only? And not -- don't clutter it with problems that you have around other witnesses. Now, you did say to the Court that Mr. Martic was going to testify, yes, indeed. You did undertake yourself, and this is where the problem comes, where you make an undertaking and you don't live up to it. You did undertake to supply, to finish Mr. Martic's 65 ter summary at the same time as you were to furnish the other summaries. Now, at the time you made that undertaking, it was quite conceivable that you are going to be in Belgrade during the recess. It's not as if it was something that was obscure to you. You just make arrangements to have somebody interview Mr. Martic while everybody else is in Belgrade so that his 65 ter statement can be prepared. In any case, you don't even need to talk to Mr. Martic to do that because he has given you instructions. You know exactly what he's going to say and from what he has instructed you just summarise that and give the 65 ter summary. You don't really need to meet him to draft that statement. You are going to be asking him questions. You know what you're going to ask him to talk about and you summarise that. From what instructions he has given you. But whatever the problems you had, my problem, and that's the problem of the Chamber, is that you made an undertaking after you'd been given indulgences, several of them. I mean, the 65 ter documents that we talked about and the witnesses we talked about, we talked about the 14th of July. This should have been filed on the 5th of July to start with and you have been getting indulgences up from that time. Now, I don't want to you say in the coming weeks we will get Mr. Martic's 65 ter summary. I would like you to give a specific date on which you say you are going to give that summary. What date can we expect? Can we expect it tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that would not be possible. Today we are sitting in the afternoon and tomorrow we are sitting in the morning, so tomorrow would not be a realistic deadline. Mr. Martic asked us to talk to him about this and today is Monday and we will inform Your Honours of everything by the end of this week. If Mr. Martic testifies, it will be at the very end of the Defence case so that the OTP will have enough time to study his summary and prepare for the cross-examination. We are fully aware of the commitment we are undertaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the Chamber is not satisfied with say we will inform the Chamber about everything by the end of the week. What does that mean? You've got to tell me when you are furnishing Mr. Martic's 65 ter summary. Give me a date and you've got to specify specifically what it is not just let us know about everything. The question specific is -- the specific question to you is when can we expect the 65 ter summary for Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we have until next Wednesday? And then we shall submit the 65 ter summary next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any comment, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that seems like an awfully long time but, you know, it's not just for us to be able to prepare to cross-examine Mr. Martic. It's so we have an understanding of the full Defence case because it's relevant to all of our preparation. But having said that, you know, if we say any earlier we probably won't get it until next Wednesday anyhow so next Wednesday is fine for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is the date next Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it's the 23rd of August, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By next Wednesday the 23rd of August the Defence is ordered to furnish the 65 ter summary for Mr. Martic. The next point you raised, Mr. Whiting -- I'm not quite sure and I'm not pre-empting your point here or trying to defend the Defence. I think they had indicated that some of these missing witnesses that they are not able to come across may have to be dropped. Are these the seven witnesses that Mr. Whiting was referring to, Mr. Milovancevic? Mr. Whiting says of the 53 witnesses that you are supposed to call, seven have no 65 ter summaries. Are those the witnesses that you say you are not able to trace and you may have to drop?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are the witnesses we were unable to trace, so very likely we will drop at least four of these witnesses. But could the Chamber and our learned friends bear in mind that our work has been derailed by the fact that one of our most important witnesses has died, and that is one of the reasons we find ourselves in the situation we are in today. However, we will inform the OTP in time about these seven witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, can I ask you to please stay to the point when we talk? The death of the one witness cannot be the reason why you are not able to trace the seven others. That could never be the reason. So don't conflate these things that are not completely unrelated. The Chamber obviously does sympathise with the Defence that one of your witnesses has passed on. Ipso facto, that is obviously going to be dropped off. The seven for whom you do not have 65 ter summaries. By when are you able to indicate whether or not you're dropping them, Mr. Milovancevic? And if you are going to drop only four of them, which four?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we shall try once more to contact these witnesses. We will do so by the end of this week. So next Wednesday, on the 23rd, we will also supply this information because by then we will have solved this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. I guess that also deals with the issue you raised, Mr. Whiting, the third one, that the Defence had undertaken that a week before trial, they would give a list of people to be dropped. Mr. Milovancevic, has the Defence made up its mind about which witnesses are going to testify in terms of 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not as yet. We have seen Your Honour's suggestions about the timetable, but we would like to respond by the 23rd of August because this has to do with the whole problem of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but remember what you have seen, in terms of our suggestion, is contained in a decision. What you need to do. And the decision does indicate that it is not for the Chamber to prosecute your case. You prosecute your case yourselves. And that's the view of the Chamber in terms of who could and who could not testify in terms of Rule 92 bis but it's still within the discretion of the Defence to decide who is going to testify in terms of Rule 92 bis. I take note that from what you are saying, you are probably indicating that you are taking into account what the Chamber indicated in the decision and hopefully you'll take it to heart when you compile your 92 bis list. Am I right, are you saying, 23rd of August, you'll also resolve the question of the 92 bis witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the exhibits that you referred to in your opening statement but which were not in the exhibit list and which you had undertaken before recess to provide copies of to the Prosecution, what is the position about them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a problem with these exhibits that they are not on our exhibit list and if we decide to use them we will submit them and we will apply for a change of the list and we will inform the OTP accordingly and submit the evidence translated, of course, as necessary. The reason why we are in this position now is precisely and literally that we have a sea of obligations that are burdening us simultaneously and we are doing our best. As regards the evidence referred to by Mr. Whiting, if that evidence is not on our list and we should decide to use them, we would apply for an extension of the 65 ter list, we will apply for a decision of the Chamber and submit the evidence to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like we are talking at cross purposes, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting, in his statement, refers specifically to exhibits that you referred to in our opening statement. Now, unless you withdraw them, you stand up formally and say I withdraw these exhibits, I'm not going to use them, these are exhibits that you have given notice of your intention to use, and he says, "I would like to have sight of these exhibits." It's not a question of as and when you, during the trial, decide to use them, you will provide him with copies of those exhibits. It's a question of you have given notice of your intention to use those exhibits. Therefore, where are they? You understand the distinction? So he's saying, "We can't wait for you to decide as you go along that you are going to use a specific exhibit when in fact you have given notice of your intention to do so. He says you've given your notice of intention, let's have it so that we can study it in the meantime. And the only way you can change that is to delete by way of withdrawal all whatever you want to delete from the list of exhibits that you referred to in your opening statement and say formally on the record, "The following that I referred to I'm not going to use any longer so you can forget about studying them." But what answer you gave is not really an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a whole series of evidence that witnesses may refer to in their testimony. They may give evidence about these documents, such as speeches that were made and various other documents. And that is why the obligation lying on the Defence regarding the documents mentioned in the opening statement is relatively complicated. We need time for that. Quite simply, within the short time we had, we did not manage to work on it as well as we would have wanted to, as the rules require, as we wanted to do. But we had a whole series of other obligations that absorbed our time. I think it would be a shame for the Defence to renounce this evidence completely, the evidence that was mentioned in the opening statement. But of course we will enable the Prosecution to familiarise themselves with every document that is available in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you understand the Chamber's point that it's not -- you're not being asked to renounce any evidence, you're just being told that if you say you're not going to use that evidence you must say up front that you're not going to use that evidence but you're not being asked to do so. Once again I don't follow your explanation, Mr. Milovancevic. Can the Chamber expect that, by the 23rd of August, you also would have dealt with this problem? Can we flag it that way? Or by when do you think you can sort it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will do our utmost to deal with this issue by the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then there are translations of exhibits in the list, some of which are dropped without specific identification of which are dropped and which are not dropped. I'm not quite sure I understood the points you raised there. Is that it --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just if we could have an indication if they already know that exhibits are going to be dropped from their list, and therefore that's why they have not translated them, if could just tell us which ones those are because they also say there are -- they are continuing to translate so it's impossible to tell just by looking at the list and see what with they have translated to determine what they've dropped. They have to tell us what they've dropped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You understand that request from your opposite number, Mr. Milovancevic? If there are any exhibits that you intend dropping, if -- the sooner you can tell them the better so that they don't have to waste time studying those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. We will do precisely that. And that work is already underway, such as translation. Whatever evidence remains on the list, we will inform our colleagues from the Prosecution in the shortest possible time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the next point related to the expert reports which you were supposed to be provided today and which are not provided. Do you have any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have submitted the military expert's report to the translation service of the Registry but it's some 250 pages and it's expected to be finished in early September. That's the information we got. If it means something to our colleagues from the Prosecution we can submit it immediately in B/C/S but I believe they needed it together with the translation. It's a technical issue that I believe depends solely on the translation service of the registry. That's as far as one expert report is concerned. The second one we did not submit due to problems we had in communication with the Registry, namely our expert has not been designated yet. The expert report is completed, by the way, but we cannot officially submit it until our expert is designated. We believe that this issue will be resolved soon and the second expert report is much shorter than the first one so we will expect it to be translated much more quickly than the first one. To avoid any confusion, the second expert report refers to the circumstances from 1990 and 1991, the application of international law, and the nature of events that took place in the territory and in the period covered by the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For my own edification, Mr. Milovancevic, what is meant by -- I don't understand -- what is meant by your second expert has not been designated by registry? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order nor an expert to appear before the Tribunal, it is necessary for the Defence to apply to the Registry with a request that this person, with their details specified, be appointed as an expert. Concerning the second expert, we made the application, put it in the locker as envisaged and when we checked before our travel, I think around the 10th, because by that time we still hadn't received a decision, it turned out that the Registry had not received our application at all. And we made the necessary steps to have this issue dealt with. However, until the expert is officially appointed by the Registry we cannot submit his report either to the Trial Chamber or to the Prosecution. That is a technical issue indeed and I believe it will be resolved soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The other witness whose report has been submitted to the Registry translation services to translate, when was it so submitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it was submitted early last week, although I can't tell you precisely. It was a very serious -- it's a very serious document and I really don't want to be wrong about the date. But I'll check it after the first break. Anyway, we submitted it for translation and we expect it to be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you expect the translation early in September?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the information we received from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't imagine there is anything you can do about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, though again the Defence undertook on the 11th of July to get this translated and have it ready for today. I don't think, if I hadn't raised it, I don't think it would have been addressed, the deadline would have just been ignored once again. So I'm a little concerned about that. There is nothing we can do about that but we will seek 30 days from the receiving of the translation of the report to study it and be able to counter it. Hopefully that won't mean any delay in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if it's 30 days from the beginning of September it shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Mr. Milovancevic, call your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I request witness Ratko Licina to be brought into the courtroom? That's our first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please, for the record, tell the Trial Chamber your full name.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Ratko Licina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you were born and where?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I was born on the 24th December 1964 in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Your ethnicity is Serb?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes, Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will now start hearing your evidence. At the very beginning I would like to ask you, since we speak the same language, and easily understand each other, to take into account the interpreters so that we have a good transcript, to make a short pause between your answers and my questions, so that the interpreters can do their job. I will try to take care of that but I will appreciate your cooperation. You told us that you were born in Gracac. It's a place in the former Yugoslav republic, Croatia, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a place in the former SFRY, the former Socialist Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the elementary and secondary school in your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. In Gracac I completed my elementary and secondary education and after the secondary school I went to do my military service in Bjeline and after that, I went to Zagreb to the school of economics of the university of Zagreb, after which I started working in a newspaper, so I spent from 1984 [Realtime transcript read in error "1994"] to 1990 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you have a degree in economics, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To give the Trial Chamber a picture of the place where you were born, I would like to say that in the atlas that we have used often during the proceedings, it's page 25, quadrant D2. That's where we can see the place called Gracac, where the witness was born.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Just a little problem here. The witness said after which I started working in a newspaper so I spent from 1994 to 1990 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It should have been 1984.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain? From 1984 I studied in Zagreb so I'm talking about the period when I studied and worked in Zagreb. I lived in Zagreb from 1984 to 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So that's when you lived in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be good to make an overview of your CV at the beginning, to see what you did from 1990s onwards. You said you were in Zagreb until 1990. And after that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Until 1994 I lived in Gracac where I was born. As I said earlier, a year after that, 1993 and 1994, I was in Bjeline doing my military service, from 1994 to 1990 I lived in Zagreb. I left Zagreb on the 17th of August 1990 and from that time, I haven't lived in Zagreb. I returned to my birthplace, Gracac, where I was until Operation Storm, the 5th of August 1995. Then together with a column of refugees, I went to Serbia. I lived for three years in Zrenjanin in Serbia and two years after that in Novi Sad, and from 1999 onwards, I have been living in Zemun a suburb of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the jobs you did, I would like to know if you had anything to do with the establishment of the SDS party and if so, what kind of connection?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I was there in the initiative council for the establishment of the Serbian party because at that time it was still not decided what the party would be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we hold it there, please? We've got an SOS from the translator's booth there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We just wanted to ask you, Your Honour, if the second microphone of the witness could be turned on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please turn on the second microphone of the witness? Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I'll repeat. I was there on the 27th of January 1990 in Donji Lapac when the initiative council for the establishment of the Serbian party met. Later it became the Serbian democratic party. That gathering was held by an unmarked pit from the Second World War in a place called Kuk and later, in Kamensko, near in Donji Lapac, that was the so-called initiative council, the initiative board for the establishment of the Serbian Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What you just said applied to the entire party. Did you also play a role in establishing the party branch in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the time I was the president of the municipal board and the founder of the party in Gracac. I was also a candidate in the elections in 1991, the first multi-party elections in Croatia for the parliament. Later on I was elected. So that's all as far as Gracac is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the SDS itself, did you hold any positions?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I was a member of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When I asked you about positions held, you mean the main and executive board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes, the main executive board of the Serbian democratic party, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that in the first multi-party elections, in 1991, you were elected a delegate to the Croatian parliament called Sabor. Did you also play a role in holding a gathering in Srb and what kind after gathering was it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes, the party initiated this gathering in Srb. Prior to that, there was an initiative to establish an association of Serbian municipalities. Perhaps we should touch upon that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this gathering in Srb, held on the 25th of July 1991, did you have a particular role in what transpired there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: On the 25th of July, 1991, a Serbian gathering was held in Srb, at which time Serbian National Council was elected with me as one of its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, Your Honour there seems to be what I think is a persist tends translation error referring to this year as 1991, the 25th of July 1991. And there is also I think another reference to 1991. Whereas I think the witness means to say 1990 but if that could be cleared up I would appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am grateful to the Bench and to my learned friend. This is about 1990. It all involves events from 1990, not 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks for letting us know. You are the one involved in this case. I thought it was Mr. Whiting. Thank you, Mr. Black. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to this position you held as a member of the Serbian National Council for which post you were elected at this assembly in SRP, did you also hold a position in the SAO Krajina government and the assembly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, I was a delegate, both in the assembly of Krajina. And in the government and later on in 1993, once again I was a candidate in the elections, both for the assembly of SAO Krajina and for other bodies. I didn't mention it in my previous answer because this assembly was founded in December 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you were a delegate, a member of the SAO Krajina assembly, and later on, in the RSK assembly and then following that in 1993 in the elections once again, you were elected a delegate, a member. Can you tell me when that was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I'm still a delegate of that assembly, when I was elected in 1993, because this assembly never stopped working. Rather it renewed its operations on the 26th of February of last year. It elected government in exile and I'm one of the members of that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you are one of the ministers of the government in exile. Which government?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in exile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If you are a member of the government in exile, can you tell us which portfolio is under your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: There are no particularly defined portfolios. I generally cover the information affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on this short summary of the positions you held, roles you played, it seems that you got involved in political events in 1990 when the first multi-party elections were held in Croatia. Can you tell us which month that was, when were the first multi-party elections held?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The elections for the Croatian parliament, as far as I can remember, were held in late April. I'm not sure about the date. That was the first round of elections and the second round was on the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Those elections were called the first multi-party elections. Can you tell us what political parties participated in the elections?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly. Up or rather by that time, a lot of political parties had been established most of them Croatian and I will list the most important ones. Croatian democratic alliance, union, held -- led by Tudjman. Croatian social-Liberal Party led by Budisa. Croatian national party led by Savka Dabcevic Kucar. Croatian Peasant Party, I think led by Cicak [phoen] and also some political organisations had been reformed. For example, the League of Communists of Croatia was transformed into the party of democratic changes and the former socialist alliance of working people of Croatia was transformed into Socialist Party. What was typical for these two parties is that they appeared together in the elections under a name of the left bloc. I think they were led by Ivica Racan. As for the Serbian parties or rather there was another small political party Yugoslav Socialist Democratic Party which later ceased to exist and later there was the Serbian Democratic Party of which I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned quite a number of parties which in their name are designated as Croatian parties and then you said there was one Serbian party as well. Do you remember when these Croatian parties were established and when was the Serbian democratic party established in Croatia, of course?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Croatian parties were established as early as 1989 whereas the Serbian Democratic Party was established quite late. I told you that the initiative council was held on the 27th of January 1990, which is to say that it was officially founded on the 17th of February 1990 in Knin. The reason for that was that previously there were obstructions to the political organisation of Serbs. They even banned cultural societies. Back in 1989, we were unable to establish Serbian cultural society in Knin. They banned it in July and it wasn't until November that this society was finally established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just before the break, and we are about to break shortly, I will put another question to you. Is it possible to give a common feature of the parties which in their name had the term "Croatian"? What was the common political feature and what was the common political goal of these parties which were founded in the course of 1989?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The common feature of all Croatian political parties was Croato-centricism and Serbo-phobia. Croato-centricism was manifested through the fact that all of these political parties, Croatian political parties, wanted to redefine Croatian political reality. The Socialist Republic of Croatia, up until that time, was in the constitution defined as a state of two peoples, and Serbian peoples. All of these political parties advocated that the constitutional status granted to the Serb people be terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I think it's time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before we continue, Witness, I'm going to ask you to slow down when giving your answer so that the interpreters can manage to interpret it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, we discussed the nature of the newly established parties in the then Republic of Croatia. You said that when it came to Croatian parties, they were Croato-centrist and Serbo-phobic. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what is it that you mean when you say that these parties were Croato-centrist?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The term Croato-centricism in my mind means, and I will repeat this once again, that it means the following: Up until that time, Croatia was defined in its constitution as a state of two nations, Serbian and Croatian. All of these Croatian political parties advocated that the rights granted to Serbs be terminated, and also other rights that we will get to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Serbo-phobia that you described, was it a result of this first feature, Croato-centricism, was it a product of that and how was it manifested?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Serbo-phobia was manifested through hatred of Serbs and fear of Serbs, fear of Serb expansion in Croatia. And it also was manifested through hatred towards Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where and when? Where did you notice such a phenomenon and in what form?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: As I said, in the beginning of my evidence, during that period of time, from 1984 until 1990, I lived in Zagreb. Croatian political parties were established in 1989 and in 1990. I was quite familiar with the then-prevailing atmosphere in Croatian media and also in various political gatherings, assemblies, and public appearances of political parties. Through that I was able to see their attitude towards Serbs. Let me give you a few examples. There was a case where an explosive was planted in the representative office of a company called Progres [phoen] from Belgrade. I think that this was in Maksimirska street in late 1989. As a result of that, the man who was head of that office suffered a heart attack and died. So he was a victim of sorts of the events at the time. The second example, in Zagreb streets at the time, one could buy metal cans, such as for example beer cans or resembling beer cans which were white in colour with a chequer-board symbol and the can was called Croatian air or it was entitled Croatian air which was supposed to denote that it was Serb-free.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in May of 1990, the first party elections were held. Can you tell us about the atmosphere that preceded the elections? Can you tell us about the pre-elections campaign? Did you follow the events from that time and did the media report on that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. In the campaign preceding the elections, the messages sent by Croatian political parties were quite negative when it came to Serbs. The slogans that they used is all Serbs should be hanging from trees and basically indicated that the Serbs would be exterminated. Let me also give you some other facts. At the time when the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union was established and I think that their founding assembly was held in Vatroslav Lisinski hall, the then president of the HDZ, Franjo Tudjman, stated that the Independent State of Croatia which was a quisling fascist creation from the Second World War, was not just a mere fascist creation but rather also an expression of thousand year long desires and aspirations of Croatian people. The second message or rather the second statement was uttered by Stjepan Mesic, who said that after they complete their political mission, all of Serbs would be able to fit under one umbrella. The third statement was also uttered by Stjepan Mesic. I think that he uttered both of these statements in Lika, in the vicinity of where I was. I think in Gospic and in Brinj. His second statement was to the effect that the Serbs could only take with them as much soil as would be stuck to their shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the shoes that he referred to were called apansi [phoen]. Apansi. Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Apansi is a traditional Serbian foot-wear. That's how I could describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The statements that you mentioned, those that stuck in your memory that were quite memorable, were stated in various rallies, rallies preceding the first multi-party elections; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic, can we get the witness to testify and not the counsel from the Bench -- from the bar? That last statement, "The statements that you mentioned, those that stuck in your memory, that were quite memorable, were stated in various rallies, rallies preceding the first multi-party elections; is that correct?" You are testifying, you are telling him what to say in answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned these statements. On what occasion were they uttered and before whom?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: As I said previously, these were statements made by high-ranking people from the HDZ, later holders of office in the Croatian state, Franjo Tudjman and Stjepan Mesic and they were uttered during the pre-election campaign in 1990. I have also mentioned the places where these things were said, in the Vatroslav Lisinski hall in Zagreb, at the HDZ founding convention. That's when Franjo Tudjman made his statement. And the other two statements I referred to are statements made by Stjepan Mesic at rallies in Brinj and Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mention Mr. Mesic, you are referring to Stjepan Mesic, are you not, who was a politician in Croatia. What post does he hold today?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to Stjepan Mesic, then a member of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, the first Prime Minister of Croatia, who was later on elected a member of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, from Croatia, and later on, on his return to Croatia, for a while he was the speaker of parliament in Croatia. Now, as far as I know, he is the president of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the political programmes and platforms of the Croatian political parties, can you tell us what their standpoint was in relation to the federal state of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: During the pre-election campaign, all these Croatian parties, the HDZ, the Croatian Social-Liberal Party, the Croatian Peasant Party, the Croatian party of rights, all advocated during the election campaign either a confederation, which would imply a reform, or dissolution. The only Croatian parties advocating in their election campaigns, the preservation of the federal state, were the left bloc parties, Party of Democratic Changes, the former communists of Ivica Racan and the other Socialist Party who were their allies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the point in time when all these parties were established, when was the Serb Democratic Party established, before or after?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The Serb Democratic Party was established after all these Croatian parties were founded and let me repeat once more, it was officially founded on the 17th of February 1990, but to make this clear to Their Honours, elections in Croatia were held in the second half of April 1990. The party was therefore established two months before the elections and a lot of work had to be done for the elections. I therefore feel that the Serb Democratic Party was established very late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please see Exhibit number 138 on the screen in this is a document dated the 16th of March 1990 and before it appears on the screen, I will explain what sort of document this is. It's a decision issued by the republican Secretariat for the judiciary and administration of the Socialist Republic of Croatia bearing the date the 6th of March 1990. Do you have the document before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the text in the upper left hand corner? Can you see who issued this document? And also can you tell us what the decision refers to? Could we scroll down a little bit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, as the document says, it was issued by the republican secretariat for the judiciary and for justice and administration, and it is a decision approving the registration of the Serb Democratic Party with the competent organ in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware that the Serb democratic party was founded on this date and that it followed the procedure described in the decision?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at paragraph 2? Paragraph 2 mentions the aims and tasks of the Serb Democratic Party. Can you read what it says?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Certainly. The aims and tasks of the Serb Democratic Party are advocating the abolition of a party state, freedom of association into political parties, the creation of conditions for the full affirmation of the spiritual and cultural identity of each Yugoslav nation, especially separately regardless of what federal unit it is in, ensuring the constitutional possibility of establishing territorial autonomies within the framework of federal units, if the population on these territories with a special ethnic composition or cultural historical identity decides this in a referendum, establishing private ownership as an element of entrepreneurship and economic progress and the spreading of market institutions and constantly caring about the situation of all the diasporas of the Serb nation in Yugoslavia, especially in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So the party was registered on this date. Could we please take a look at the statement of reasons for this decision? In English it's on page 2, Your Honours. Could we scroll up a little bit? Could we look at the next page? Can we scroll up? Yes. On page 2, at the top of the page, it says that the application is well-founded. Can you read the text below that sentence, which contains the statement of reasons as to why the statement -- the request is seen to be well-founded?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: In the proceedings the following was established: First, that on the 17th of February 1990, a founding assembly, a constituent assembly was held at which the Serb Democratic Party was established or constituted. Secondly, that the Statute of the Serb Democratic Party, which was adopted at the assembly held on the 17th of February 1990, is in compliance with the provisions of the law on social organisations and associations of citizens. Furthermore, that all the legal conditions for the inscription of the Serb Democratic Party into the register of social organisations have been fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take a look at the bottom of the document? In the lower right-hand corner there is a seal and the -- it also says who signed this decision.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So who issued this document, in fact?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, the signature is the republican secretary, Mr. Ivan Fumic and the seal is that of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, the republican Secretariat for justice and administration in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side we see to whom the decision was delivered. Could you read points 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: 1, to the Serb Democratic Party in Knin, at the address Jovomir [phoen] Dragovico street 22. And secondly to the republican Secretariat of the Interior for its information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. What we have seen in this document, is this the procedure envisioned for the registration of any political party, including the Serb Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. This was then the standard procedure for registering a political organisation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The document can be removed from the screen. It has been admitted into evidence. In view of the fact that you were one of the founders of the Serb Democratic Party, in the Statute and programme of the party, was there anything that was not in line with the democratic principles and the social principles accepted at the time in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: No. There wasn't and could not have been because it would not have been registered otherwise. As we can see from this document, the party was registered, which means that it was correct in all respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The reason I put this question to you was that we have heard statements here to the effect that this was a nationalist party. In your work as someone active in the party from 1990 to 1995, did you see anything that might be described as nationalistic in the work of the party?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: No. The Serb Democratic Party could not be referred to as a nationalist party. It was the national party of the Serbs in Croatia but certainly not nationalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As you are one of the founders of the party, can you tell us what the immediate cause was for the establishment of the party at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The immediate cause was the need to organise the Serb people into Croatia politically. Up to that time, the Serbs for the most part were politically organised in the League of Communists of Croatia. However, it was transformed and as we shall see later, it betrayed its principles and the promises it had made during the election campaign. It was therefore urgently necessary for the Serb people in Croatia to have a Serbian political party established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the point in time when the party was founded, the first multi-party elections in Croatia were held in April and May 1990, can you tell us which party won the elections and what the results of the Serb Democratic Party were, of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The elections in Croatia were held at the republican and local levels. They were majority elections. The party which won a decisive victory was the Croatian Democratic Union, because it had the majority in all three councils of the Croatian parliament. At that time the Croatian parliament consisted of three councils, the social political council, the council of municipalities and the council of associated labour. The HDZ, as far as I can recall, had a two-thirds majority in two of these three councils. The only one it did not have a two-thirds majority in was the council of associated labour. As I said, the Serb Democratic Party was established late, only two months before the elections, on the 17th of February 1990. And in many Serb towns and villages, it had not had time to establish its committees, where it had it won. And the SDS then existed only in the municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and southern Lika. It won five seats in the Croatian parliament, three representatives from Knin municipality went to the parliament, one from Donji Lapac and I from Gracac. As for elections for the local parliaments, the SDS won an absolute majority in the municipalities of Knin, Gracac and Donji Lapac, and it also held power, together with other assemblymen in the municipalities of Benkovac, Obrovac, Korenica and Glina and I think Vojnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've given us a very detailed reply to this question. Maybe in order to understand the overall situation in the Croatian parliament at the time, it might be a good idea if you were to tell us how many Members of Parliament there were. You said that the SDS won five seats. How did the Serb electorate vote in Croatia, if you have any information about this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. The Croatian parliament, as far as I can recall, had about 350 seats. Of that, there were about 40 or 45 Serbs, five of us from the SDS and the remaining 40 were mostly from the so-called left bloc, which means Ivica Racan's party, the League of Communists transformed into the Party of Democratic Changes and the Socialist Party, I think its president was called Madzar and at the elections they said they were in favour of the survival of the joint federal state. However, the majority of Serbs, especially in northern Lika, Kordun, Banija, western Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia and Baranja, as the SDS did not have its candidates in those areas, voted for these representatives. Later on, it turned out that the left bloc abandoned its pre-election promises and joined Franjo Tudjman and his HDZ in implementing Croatian independence. It therefore betrayed the votes of the Serbian voters it had gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To avoid any vagueness in the transcript, when you say there were 45 Serbs in the parliament, are you referring to Members of Parliament, deputies?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. I am referring to deputies or Members of Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the length of your reply, could you just very briefly repeat the Serb Democratic Party had how many Members of Parliament?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The Serb Democratic Party had five Members of Parliament,. Five seats in parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The party of democratic changes, the former League of Communists of Croatia, headed by Ivica Racan had how many seats in parliament?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I can't be precise but around 40. This is approximate. It's one or two more or less but that was the approximate number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These 45 deputies or Members of Parliament, were people for whom the Serb electorate had voted, is that what you said just a while ago?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As the Croatian Democratic Union won a majority in the Croatian parliament, and the elections were completed in early May, what were the political developments that followed, for the benefit of Their Honours? How can we best understand the situation with regard to the position of the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, the status of the Serbs in Croatia continued to deteriorate. Practically there was ethnic cleansing of Serbs from all state institutions, primarily the police and the state organs, as well as public companies, companies established by the state or municipal organs. An illustration of this is, for example, when in May, during the Dynamo/Red Star soccer game a large number of Serbs, who had been policemen, lost their jobs and later it turned out that they had been set up so that those people could be fired because there was an incident that happened at that soccer game.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned something that will be hard for Their Honours to understand. So this was a game between two soccer clubs. Where were they from? You say there was an incident. Who was blamed for that incident?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: This was a game between Dinamo and Red Star. Dinamo is a club from Zagreb. The Red Star is a club from Belgrade. Most Serbs from the Krajina supported the Red Star. There was an incident and the soccer game was interrupted. Because a certain number of Serbs were employed in the police, after that soccer match, most of them were replaced because of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to the problem of labour relations. Do you know anything about the political changes such as changes to the constitution that took place at that time after the first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. Huge changes occurred in politics. After winning a land side victory, the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, moved on to change the constitution. The amendments to the constitution were adopted in July 1990. Already then, we saw the first signs that a new constitution would be adopted and in that constitution, Croatia would be defined as a state of the Croatian people only. Serbs did not accept that. Serbs for their part moved to organise themselves as they had a legal right to, and in the municipalities that I enumerated, where the SDS won power, formed a union, an association of municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika that was later joined by other municipalities. The Croatian assembly kept avoiding legal procedures in amending the constitution because it refused to form a commission for the equality of nations and ethnicities that had existed earlier in the Croatian parliament, and every topic that related to equality among nations and ethnicities had to be discussed by that commission. That commission however was not elected until the end of 1990, so that some legal changes and amendments to the constitution and also the new constitution of Croatia adopted in December 1990 did not have a chance to go through this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the intent of the new authorities of Croatia to define Croatia as a state of the Croatian people only. Can you tell us why this was so important to the Serb people in Croatia, to prevent these changes from happening and how did the Serb people react their through legal representatives?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I don't want to go too deep into the historical background but in all constitutions starting from 1945 to 1990, Serbs were a constituent nation and of course they wanted it to stay that way. Imagine if something like that happened in some European country, Switzerland or Belgium or some other multi-ethnic European state, just imagine if one of the nations were to be deleted from the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serb representatives, the representatives of the Serb people in Croatia, react to the proposed amendments to the constitution? Did they make counterproposals and if so, what kind of counterproposals?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I was a member of the Croatian parliament and I can say that there was not a single proposal from the Serbian Democratic Party or any Serbian MP that was accepted. This voting machinery just outvoted us time and time again, although it didn't have the right to because we were not a minority. We were a nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why it was so important for Serbs in Croatia to preserve their status of nation in matters decisive for the fate of the state and the people?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: In the past century, Croat Serbs suffered two major pogroms and both happened in very similar situations. The first time was in 1941 to 45, during the times of the Independent State of Croatia when Serbs were outlawed and the second time was recently, in 1991 to 1995, and it was logical and vital for us to preserve our status of nation because if we didn't, we thought we would -- we thought that that -- that there would be open season on us and indeed that's the way it was, the way it turned out to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The proposed amendments to the constitution of Croatia envisaged that Serbs would get the status of a minority. Under the constitution, can a minority decide the status of a state or does that right belong only to nations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: No. A minority cannot do that. As defined by the constitution, the constituent nature of a people belongs only to a nation, not to a minority, and if the Serbs lost the status of a nation they would lose the right automatically to decide what kind of state they want to live in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that all proposals of Serb MPs in the Croatian parliament were rejected, one after another. What were the activities of Serb representatives in that month of July? Was there anything note worthy?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Among the most important events in July 1990 was the assembly in Srb on the 25th of July, when the Serb National Council was established and the declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serbian people was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we see on the monitor Exhibit number 141? Before we see it on the screen, I'll say that it's a declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people adopted on the occasion of the Serb assembly held in Srb on the 25th of July 1990. In the introductory part of this declaration, Mr. Licina, the latter part of this introduction, it says that the Serb people living in the historic territories unified by the present borders, the Socialist Republic of Croatia, adopts and promulgates at this Serbian Assembly held in Srb on the 25th of July 1990, the following declaration. Can you read for us paragraph 1? The first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Within the borders of the Socialist Republic of Croatia which is also the state of the Serb people living in SR Croatia, the Serb people is, on the basis of its geographic, historic, social and cultural peculiar its a sovereign people with all the rights inherent in the sovereignty of a nation. The Serb people has every right to opt for a confederative or a federal state form together with the Croatian people or independently when a new relations are established in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this assembly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. I was there on the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this para one of this declaration, there is reference to the sovereignty of the Serb people living at that time in the Republic of Croatia and their right to opt for a confederation or a federation is emphasised. Was that one of the main reasons why the Serb people, the Serb population in Croatia, and their representatives, insisted on that sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Certainly. Serbs had to act in this way because they knew what could happen to them. I just want to inform the Honourable Trial Chamber briefly of one matter. In the state of Croatia prior to the First World War, which was called Banovina Croatia and which encompassed approximately the territory of today's Croatia, but also including a territory populated by Croats in western Herzegovina, in that Banovina Croatia, there were 37 per cent of Serbs. After the genocide in the Second World War and the fleeing of refugees, the population of Serbs was reduced to 12 per cent. At least that is the figure that is being used today. So this is why the Serbs didn't want to be outvoted in certain bodies just by using majority voting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In para 2 of this declaration on sovereignty and autonomy, there is reference to the right to autonomy. Can you read for us this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: On the basis of its sovereignty the Serb people in Croatia is entitled to autonomy. The essence of that autonomy will depend on whether Yugoslavia is constituted as a federation or a confederation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What political arrangements were envisaged for either of these options?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Since I was a member of the party that politically inspired this document, I can confirm that it was our position that if Croatia should remain part of the federation of Yugoslavia, if Yugoslavia remains a federation, Serbs would want and advocate cultural autonomy. However, if Yugoslavia is constituted as a confederation, then Serbs would want territorial autonomy and Serbs would anyway have the right to express themselves and their desires as to which state and what kind of state they want to live in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to have that possibility to express themselves, what was it necessary for the Serbian people to preserve? Which feature? Which capacity?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: It was essential for us to preserve our capacity of nation, a constituent nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This declaration was mentioned many times and it is indeed curious, in view of certain elements. Let us look at this paragraph 2 that envisages autonomy. In both options confederate or federal, would the Serb people seek anything other, anything more, than autonomy?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: No, preceding from those principles, we wanted cultural autonomy, redefining our right to our own language, in the case of a federation. However, if there should be a confederation, we wanted territorial autonomy but we did not make any moves to secede before that happened in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Item 3 mentions that the representatives of the Serb Assembly and it says that the representatives of the Serb nation should establish a Serb Assembly and that the executive organ of that assembly would be the Serbian National Council. Is that the same council that you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Serbian National Council consisted of Serb deputies in the assembly, plus the presidents of municipalities where Serbs constituted a majority and the president of the SDS and some representatives of the Serbian orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out item 4 of this declaration? What does it say about a right of the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Item 4 reads, Serbian National Council has a right to organise a plebiscite for the Serb nation to express their will on all issues which are vital for its position in Croatia and Yugoslavia as well as all other issues which concerned the exercise of Serbian sovereignty and autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this declaration also include the relations or the attitude of Serb representatives towards the constitutional amendments? Could you please read out item 6?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Item 6, Serbian Assembly in its session in Srb on the 25th of July 1990 hereby declares null and void, as far as the Serbian nation is concerned, all constitutional and legal amendments which deny its sovereignty as a nation and minimise its autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your view, did this also include any intention to secede from the territory of Croatia, to expel another nation just because of the fact that they are of a different ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: None of the items of this declaration contains anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read out item 7, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Item 7, Serb nation in Croatia does not seek anything above the rights which have been enjoyed for a long time by other contemporary nations in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this declaration reflects your political views and attitude towards the status of Serb nation in Croatia and Yugoslav crisis?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can take this document off the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
