utterances.text: As for the provision of this declaration about the right of the Serbian National Council to schedule or to organise a plebiscite or a referendum where Serb people would be able to vote on their status within Yugoslavia, do you know whether such a decision was passed after all by the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. The assembly was held on the 25th of July and several days later, I'm not quite sure which date it was, Serbian National Council held its first session in Knin. The first decision adopted was the one on the right of Serbs to express their will on autonomy. It was scheduled for the 19th of August, which is the Orthodox holiday of transfiguration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So far, Mr. Licina, you mentioned autonomy in your evidence quite frequently. The term itself denotes what, in your view, that a territory belongs to a state and is within that state or is seceding from a state?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: In my view, autonomy means that a territory exists within a state but with special political and other rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is this what the Serb representatives and Serb people in Croatia at the time sought?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs advocated their right to autonomy and they wanted it to exist on multi-levels, which is to say they wanted cultural or territorial autonomy depending of -- depending on the form in which the future state was to exist, confederate or federal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we see document from the 65 ter list marked 431? Before the document comes up on the screen, in order to be as efficient as possible, I will tell you that this is a newspaper article dated the 31st of July. This is the article written by Tanjug which was the news agency of Yugoslavia. The time is 1739. This is a newspaper report on the decision adopted by the Serbian National Council. I would like to hear your comment. I don't know whether I was sufficiently accurate. This document comes from the 65 ter list and is marked 431. Yes. There it is. This is the document, or rather a news report. Could you please read out the first two paragraphs of this document?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: "Accordance with the decision adopted in a recent assembly of Serbs at the constituent assembly held this evening, Serbian National Council took the decision to call for a referendum at which the Serbs in Croatia would express their views as to whether they wanted autonomy. President of the Serbian Democratic Party, Jovan Raskovic pointed out that this would be a response to Croatian leaders who claim that only a very small number of Orthodox residents in Croatia desire Serb autonomy within the republic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did this report accurately reflect what was discussed at this session of the Serbian National Council and did you take part in adopting this decision?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The news report mentions a statement by Jovan Raskovic. What did Mr. Raskovic say there when mentioning the reasons for organising the referendum?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Croatian authorities at the time attempted to establish contact with the SDS. However, the SDS was unable to accept the constitutional redefining of Croatia. Following that, they tried to present the SDS as a minority, which was formally the -- formally the case but only due to procedural reasons. We were unable to establish the party in -- on time. And this was a good opportunity to show what was the political will of the Serbs in Croatia, and what was their attitude towards these demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please read out the following two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The referendum is to be held in Croatia between the 19th of August and the referendum is to be held in Croatia between the 19th of August and the 2nd of September of this year. Serbian National Council in today's session rejected all amendments to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia adopted by the Croatian National Assembly. The assembly also rejected the use of Croatian national symbols, especially coat of arms as symbols of the Republic of Croatia especially in areas where Serbs constitute majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This last sentence of the report saying that the president of the National Assembly of Knin, Milan Babic was elected president of the council, was that statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: No, because formally, it should say that he was president of Knin municipality. That was his formal position. And in the preceding paragraphs, there is a formal error as well because it should say Republic of Croatia and the Croatian assembly should be referred to as Sabor which was the formal name of the parliament. The essence is accurate but some formal titles and names are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move to have this document from the 65 ter list admitted into evidence as Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document will become Exhibit 871.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you gave us your view of the reasons due to which Mr. Raskovic, who is a professor and a member of the academy of arts and sciences and also a founder of the SDS, claimed that the statements of Croatian authorities were incorrect when they said that it was only a Serb minority that wanted the autonomy. Let us now talk about the elections. What happened with the representatives elected by the Serb voters who were members of the former League of Communists of Croatia, the newly renamed Party of Democratic Changes led by Ivica Racan. You started talking about this but let us go back to this issue?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The Party of Democratic Changes and that entire left bloc led by Ivica Racan in the pre-election campaign came up with slogans reflecting that they were in favour of a joint state of Yugoslavia, a federal state. These messages and slogans were accepted first and foremost by the Serbs, and as such the Party of Democratic Changes was the second-strongest party in the Croatian parliament, owing to a large extent to the votes of Serbs. However, the party was abandoned by its leadership as soon as they entered the parliament, and the members of the party changed their platform and completely accepted the political platform of the HDZ and Franjo Tudjman. Thus, a government of national unity was elected. Its vice-president was Zdenko Tomac, who was a highly placed member of the Party of Democratic Changes, and Spegelj, who was also a member of that party, was elected to another high post in the government. As a result, the remaining members left that party and joined the SDS, so that dramatically changed the political scene in Croatia after these first multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to this political change that you just described, this change in the attitude of the Party of Democratic Changes which won the votes of the majority of Serbs in Croatia, can you please briefly describe what this change in their platform entailed? What did they support before the elections and what after?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Before the elections, the Party of Democratic Changes, at least formally, supported a federal state. Following the elections, they completely changed their political platform and, just like the HDZ, first they advocated the confederation, and then secession. This was manifested through the attitude and conduct of their members, first as parliament -- Members of Parliament and later on as members of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that the representatives who were on the ballot of the Party of Democratic Changes following the election started joining the ranks of SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will discuss the plebiscite and referendum in greater detail later on, the one that was scheduled to be held between the 19th of August and the 2nd of September, and the Serbs there were supposed to vote on the autonomy. Now, please tell us this: How did the Serbs in Croatia vote in that referendum when it came to Serb autonomy?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The Serb residents in Croatia voted for Serb autonomy in great numbers. I think that the number was over 97 per cent, so an overwhelming majority. I'm not sure about the exact number but it could probably be looked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the Serb National Council, on the 31st of July, 1990 scheduled this referendum, was such a political decision unconstitutional, unlawful or illegal?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: No. It was not unlawful. The referendum or plebiscite is the most democratic form of expressing voters' will, so there should be nothing unlawful or illegal about it. It is unlawful to use force and there was nothing violent about this. This was just a democratic mechanism for expressing the will of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So they were expressing the will on the Serb autonomy, Serb autonomy of Serbian people within Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. This referendum was not to define this autonomy, to specify whether it was a cultural or any other sort of autonomy. It was just for them to vote about the right to autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained earlier that there was no success in attempts to find a political, peaceful resolution. Can you please tell us what was the reaction of Croatian authorities to decisions adopted by the Serbian National Council to hold a referendum between the 19th of August and the 2nd of September?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The then Croatian authorities tried to prevent this referendum by use of force. This is evident because on the 17th of August, they moved with APCs and helicopters in an attempt to prevent this referendum from taking place. They moved in the direction of Benkovac, Gracac and other Serb-populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We heard some other explanations given about these events; we heard it here during this trial. Based on what, Mr. Licina, do you believe that the Croatian authorities used force in order to prevent the referendum from taking place?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, I can explain based on my personal experience. The 17th of August was the last day of my residence in Zagreb. That was the last day I went to work in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. Could you please give us the year?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The 17th of July, 1990. On that day, it was Friday, so I was on my way to go home to my mother and especially since the referendum was scheduled to be held that weekend, so I was travelling home in a bus from Zagreb to Gracac, which is a distance of 220 kilometres. 70 kilometres prior to Gracac lies Korenica, which is another municipality, and I saw Croatian APCs there. I saw people who came out to protest. There were Croatian APCs there. The bus stopped, and I spoke through the window with some people outside of the bus and they told me that the barricades had been erected near Gracac and that these units were at the ready to raid Gracac. Since the bus turned off that highway between Zagreb and Zadar, it was rather turned away to -- and took another road. I reached Gospic and then from Gospic I took the train to Gracac and arrived there in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Licina. Before I go on with my questions, for Their Honours to understand this more easily, on page 25 of the atlas, in square D1, in the middle, there is a place called Titova Korenica. That's the place the witness is referring to in describing his trip from Zagreb to Gracac. Gracac is in the 2 and Zagreb is to the north. You say you entered Titova Korenica and saw an APC. What is an APC, to avoid any misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, that is what we call a police combat vehicle. It's on wheels, not on caterpillar tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So is it a passenger vehicle, is it armoured?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: It's armoured and it has a weapon. I think it's some sort of machine-gun, but I don't know exactly what sort of weapon it is. That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And this happened on the 17th of August?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes, the 17th of August, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was happening in other parts of the Krajina or the Socialist Republic of Croatia on that day? Did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: At the same time something else was happening. In those municipalities where the Serbs were in the majority, the Croatian authorities, in some smaller areas of those municipalities, where there were Croat populations, established some small police stations, police outposts. For example, in Obrovac municipality, this happened in Krusevo. In Knin municipality such a police station was opened in Kijevo. In Titova Korenica municipality, I think there was a police station in Podlapaca. And in Glina municipality, I think there was one in Vidusevac. At the same time, the regular police stations, which were in the municipal towns I mentioned, Gracac, Obrovac, Benkovac, Knin and Korenica, weapons of the reserve police force were taken from those police stations. At the same time, they were creating and arming new police units in places where previously there had been no police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Serb population to such events? You mentioned something to do with Gracac. Do you have information about other places?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I know that in Gracac, because I used to go there over the weekend and later on I lived there, the people were very upset, and justifiably so. Overnight the chiefs of those police stations took out weapons and these people were nearly lynched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about barricades and, if you did, what was this about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The barricades were erected on the 17th of August, because Croatia, as I said, had moved its police forces. New police stations were being opened in the places I mentioned. During the night, weapons were taken from Serb municipalities, and, of course, the people were very tense or very upset.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see any barricades? Who erected them? What were they made of? Were the people manning them armed or unarmed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, the barricades typically were erected where the people organised. They were self-organised. They would chop down a few trees or put sandbags across the road, and then they would stand there with their own personal or hunting weapons to try to prevent incursions into our villages. Why did this happen? Well, quite logically, the Serbs had vivid memories of what had happened to them 50 years before. They had been slaughtered in many places, their numbers reduced, so it was quite logical that people should be afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the 17th of August, which year were these barricades erected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 17th of August, 1990, Your Honours. All of this happened in 1990. Everything we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This may be a convenient moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Licina, we were talking about barricades being erected. The term "log revolution" has been used. Have you ever heard of such a term?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I have heard of the term "log revolution." This was a pejorative name for the Serb barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You were one of the founders and leaders of the SDS in your town. You say that you were on your way back to Gracac from Zagreb on the 17th of August and that you saw barricades along the way. Did you participate in the erection of these barricades or did the SDS participate in it? Can you tell us something about this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: On that day, I was on my way from Zagreb, so I couldn't have participated in the erection of the barricades because I wasn't there. This was done by self-organised local people. There was no organisation carried out by a party or anything like that. It was simply that people were frightened, they were under pressure, they were afraid because police stations in Serb municipalities had been disarmed, new police stations were being established, and people were afraid. So the emergence of the barricades was simply a logical step.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have had occasion to hear different interpretations, that these barricades were used to mistreat the non-Serb population, as it is referred to, that their role was different. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: No, I know nothing like that. The role of the barricades was defensive. A barricade in itself is a defensive device. It's not used to attack but to defend from an attack, so it cannot constitute a threat to anyone. Whether there were any individual excesses, no one can say. There may have been individual excesses, but in general, the barricades were a way for the Serbs to protect themselves from what was about to happen to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there barricades in other places besides Gracac? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. There were barricades around Gracac, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, around most of those Serb municipalities at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw Croatian armoured personnel carriers in the Titova Korenica area. Were there such attempts in places around Zadar, such as Benkovac and Obrovac? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. The area we are referring to, when you set out from Zagreb, from the north, you go through Korenica and Gracac. If you're coming from the side of Dalmatia, from Zadar, Sibenik or Split, you first come to Obrovac, then Benkovac, then Knin. And as far as I know, the same things happened in Benkovac. Weapons were taken away, the people became afraid, and as far as I knew, I think a helicopter of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior set out in the direction of Benkovac but a JNA plane turned it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about a state of war being declared in Knin on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: On the 17th of August, 1990, as I said, that was the day I arrived, and I heard from others that the then-president of Knin municipality, Milan Babic, had proclaimed a state of war. He later denied this, but I heard this from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Barricades were erected, you say, and after all this, was a referendum held and who participated in it. Where was it held, under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The referendum was held in all Serb municipalities where the Serbs were in power. As far as I know, this was in the Dalmatian area, in Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Drnis municipalities. In Lika, it was in Gracac, Donji Lapac, and Korenica municipalities, and then in Kordun and Banija as well. The referendum was also held in some places where the Serbs were in the minority, but it was prevented there. There was violence, even burning of ballots. In areas where the Serbs were in a significant minority, amounting to 30 or 40 per cent of the population, the referendum was prevented and especially so in towns. I wish to remind Their Honours that apart from the areas in which the Serbs were in the majority, there were very many Serbs living in the urban parts of Croatia, in Zagreb, Split and Rijeka. According to our information, there were over 100.000 Serbs in Zagreb alone and their voting was interrupted, prevented, and that is why the referendum was extended until the 2nd of September. 90 per cent of the referendum was completed that weekend, the 19th, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As the referendum was envisioned as the expression of the will of the Serb population, in the areas where the Serbs were in the majority in the then Republic of Croatia, was there any ban, prohibition or limitation on members of other ethnic groups to vote in the referendum or were they prohibited from voting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: No. There was no prohibition. People came out and voted. I even know of some Croats living in Gracac who came and voted at this referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the vast majority of Serbs voted in favour of Serb autonomy and sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the representatives of the Serb people have occasion to present the results of the referendum to the Croatian parliament and authorities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The referendum was held on the 19th of August, 1990, and a few days later, I think on the 26th of August, there was a session of the Croatian parliament, and the evening before this, the Executive Board of the Serb Democratic Party held a session. It was decided that one representative, and that was me, should go to the parliamentary session and present the standpoints and conclusions from the assembly in Srb, and as 90 per cent of the referendum had already been completed, as far as numbers go, we were also to present the results of the referendum. On that occasion, I went to the parliament and I presented all this. At that session, there was quite a lot of pressure. The entire state leadership of Croatia was there, with Franjo Tudjman at their head. The previous Prime Minister, Stipe Mesic, was elected as a member of the Presidency of the SFRY and Josip Manolic was put in his place, and the previous member of the Presidency, Stipe Suvar was replaced. I was there at that session, and I presented the standpoints of our party and the decisions reached that because of the actions of the Republic of Croatia, this was actually voting, although we called it a referendum, and they had tried to prevent it by force. And for this reason, I told them that the Serb Democratic Party was suspending its participation in the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After this information and everything that happened, were any political agreements reached? Did the situation improve or did it deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, the situation deteriorated. The Croatian authorities, instead of inviting us for talks, failed to respond. The crisis continued. In September, there was an incursion by the Croatian police in Petrinja, and the people in Petrinja municipality, that's a municipality with a Serb majority in the area of Banija, when the people who were frightened of these police forces fled to the JNA barracks called Vasil Gacesa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me, sorry, I don't understand what you mean by "the Croatian authorities, instead of inviting us for talks, failed to respond." Respond to what, if they are supposed to invite you for talks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, until then, Croatia was trying to make out that the position of the Serbian Democratic Party was a position of the minority of the Serb people in Croatia. However, with the turnout at the referendum being so huge and with the result being what it was, legitimised our position as representatives of Serbs in Croatia and as such we expected the Croatian authorities to talk to us, to talk to us about stopping further conflicts and redefining our relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but what were they expected to respond to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were supposed to respond to our position that, well, nigh, all the Serb people in Croatia were in favour of sovereignty and their opposition to Croatia becoming a state of the Croat people only. Those views of ours were also confirmed and legitimised at the referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the question just asked of you by the Judge, you mentioned in your answers that after the first multi-party elections held in April and May 1990, an initiative was made to amend the Croatian constitution whereby the Serbs would be thrown out of it as a people, as a nation. And when you were answering the question of Judge Moloto what the Croatian authorities were to respond to, can you tell us what the Serb expectations were? Did they expect that there would or would not be by changes to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The Serbs did not want the constitution to be amended in that way. And with that referendum they clearly made it known that there could be no constitutional amendments reducing the Serb people to the status of a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the then Croat authorities did not respond to your demands as representatives of the Serb people and you mentioned the situation in Petrinja. Who intervened in Petrinja and why did the people run to the barracks, to the army barracks? Who were they fleeing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: In Petrinja there was a raid by the police forces of Croatia and there was some fighting or something like that around the police station, and the people panicked, seeing the general situation in town, and they fled to the army barracks, the barracks of the JNA, called Vasil Gacesa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that initiative of the Croatian authorities aimed at disarming police stations in majority-Serb localities. In addition to that, were there any changes to the size and composition of the units of the MUP, Ministry of Interior, of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: As far as I know, Croatia built up its police force by about 100.000. They employed 50.000 new policemen and dismissed a lot of Serbs. Until then, the requirements for a policeman were to have no criminal record, no ongoing prosecution, but at that time, those requirements no longer applied. The only thing required of a new recruit was to be a Croat and to be as extreme as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that a requirement was to have no ongoing prosecution and no criminal record. You talked -- you meant prior requirements for somebody to be employed as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. In order for somebody to be employed as a policeman, one of the requirements was to have no criminal record. With these new members of the police force, that particular rule was not observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to beefing up the police force, you mentioned some measures applying to police stations, the disarming of police stations in certain localities, such as Lovinac. When did those changes in Lovinac occur? You mentioned the elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Lovinac, Sveti Rok, Lisica and Licko Cerijev [phoen] are all localities within the municipality of Gracac where I was head of the Municipal Board of the SDS and where I was also elected as MP to the Croatian parliament. At the first founding session of the local municipal parliament, they walked out of the local parliament, and they no longer participated in its work. And immediately after that, a police station was set up and we had no passage through a part of our municipality. Let me emphasise that as you go from Lovinac towards Gospic there is a line of Serb villages that also conducted a referendum in June and July concerning their joining to Gracac. This was a completely legal referendum, and Gracac reacted positively to their referendum. And after the legal term, the legal delay, expired, those municipalities became part of Gracac. However, we could not function as a single municipality because you couldn't reach one part of that municipality from another part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You told us about these changes from April to May 1990, and you used terms "we" and "they," talking about the local parliaments, et cetera. To avoid confusion, what were the election results in Gracac, what parties participated and who were "they" and who were you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I was talking about the local elections. The municipality of Gracac had 78 per cent, I believe, Serbs, and around 20 per cent Croats, approximately. And at those local elections, the Serb Democratic Party came out victorious. We had an absolute majority. There were some independent candidates from SK -- that is the League of Communists of Croatia, the Party for Democratic Changes and some other parties from the areas of those two -- four municipalities such as Lovinac, Sveti Rok, Lisica and Licko Cerijev. At the first session, although we invited them and suggested that one of them co-chair the founding assembly, they walked out and they did not participate in the work of the local parliament. That's what I meant. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that you've just explained to us the political representatives of the Croat population in Gracac municipality were elected on their own lists, they refused any further cooperation with Serbs, and they walked out of the local parliament of Gracac?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. That happened back in May 1990. I don't know whether the first session took place on the 29th or the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned a new police station was set up. What do you mean by "new"? Did it exist before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Until then, we only had a Secretariat in Gracac or, rather, the police station, the only police station, was in Gracac. Only in municipal centres did you have a police station. In other localities, no. However, when the new authorities came into power at the republican level, they set up a new police station in the locality of Lovinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us return to our general topic. You said the elections were over. You had a seat in parliament, September came, October, November 1990, and when I asked you whether the situation was deteriorating or not, you said that it did get worse. What happened in December 1990? What political events marked that period and had an influence on future developments?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: That period from September to December was marked by a deterioration of the situation. In December, in my opinion, two important things happened. Croatia adopted its constitution and SAO Krajina was proclaimed. The Autonomous District of Krajina. There were deliberations about the Croatian constitution although some rules were disregarded; namely, that it pass through the commission on equality of nations and ethnicities. Why was this important? Since there were 350 or so MPs in total in the parliament, and only around 45 Serbs, they could always be easily outvoted. That's why, until then, in all earlier Croatian parliaments, there was this commission for equality of nations and ethnicities made up of Croats and Serbs together. All issues that related to equality, the status of a constituent nation, et cetera, had to go through that commission. However, the new Croatian government did not elect this commission and all constitutional amendments were enacted without being discussed by that commission. And decisions in the commission were supposed to be taken by consensus. That is one way in which the Serbs were completely betrayed and tricked in this procedure. In order to prevent this, because it was obvious that Croatia had no intention of talking to us anymore, and in line with the will of the Serbian people, expressed both at the assembly in Srb and at this referendum, the Association of Municipalities of Northern Lika -- Northern Dalmatia and Lika, Serbs proclaimed the Autonomous Region of Krajina on the 19th of December, 1990, which is the day of the patron saint, Nicholas, and in the same month, the new Croatian constitution was promulgated. The parliament session began on the 22nd December and the constitution was proclaimed on the Catholic Christmas day, the 25th of December, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This new Croatian constitution defined Croatia as the state of which people?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The new Croatian constitution defined Croatia as the state of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In all prior constitutions after the Second World War, after 1945, Serbs and Croats had equal status of constituent peoples in Croatia. Serbs, however, lost that status with this constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. This was in violation of all the rights that Serbs enjoyed until that time. That right was guaranteed to the Serbs by the ZAVNOH, which was the anti-fascist council set up by -- set up after the Second World War because the Serbs had a very large contribution in liberating Croatia and the territory of the former Yugoslavia from the Nazis. When the anniversary of Bleiburg was celebrated, that is the anniversary of the pogrom of anti-fascist forces in the territory of Austria in 1945, at that commemoration held under the aegis of the parliament of Croatia, the Croatian government, and the president, Stipe Mesic, an important thing was mentioned; namely, that the so-called Kriz road, there were 200.000 Croats and 500.000 residents. That's the way of the cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You told us already that the new Croatian constitution was adopted on the 25th of December. What was the Serb response to that? And what happened on the 19th December, 1990? What was established?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: On the 19th of December, as I said earlier, the Serb Autonomous District of Krajina was established. It was formed through an initiative of the association of Northern Dalmatia and Lika municipalities that had expanded by then, and that's when this autonomous district was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Might I ask a question? Within the terms of the old constitution for the federation, how would a constituent people have been defined? And could you tell me also what would determine and distinguish a minority, by way of definition as well as the consequences of that definition? Could you do that for me, please? Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm talking about the constitutions of Croatia, not about federal constitutions. And until that time, in all constitutions of Croatia, Serbs and Croats were both at the same footing, defined as constituent peoples. At the federal level, I believe the constitution stipulated that the Socialist Federal Republic Yugoslavia was a state of Slovene, Croatian, Serb, Muslim, Montenegrin and other nations, the peoples of which there was a state were defined in the constitution. But I was talking about one federal unit in Yugoslavia and its constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. And I do stand corrected. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I want to hear then what is the definition under the Croatian constitution. Answer the questions within the terms of the Croatian constitution then, having so corrected me very kindly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the constitution of Croatia, it was specified or, rather, the new constitution defined Croatia as the state of the Croatian people. The constitution so far specified that the Croatian state was the state of Croats and Serbs in Croatia and both of them were on equal footing. That would be similar to the situation in Belgium where you have Flemish people and Walloons who have equal rights; or, for example, the situation in Switzerland where you have three or four equal nations. Serbs and Croats were constituent nations within Croatia. Had they been a minority, then the situation would have been different. Then they would have not had all the rights, and there could have been a secession without approval of the Serbs. However, if Serbs are a constituent nation, then their consent is required for concession because a nation comes above a republic. This is the essence of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, this political decision to establish the SAO Krajina, that is to say Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, this area was defined as part of Croatia. Do you know which laws were applied in the territory of SAO Krajina? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I think that all of the laws in existence until then were applied in relation to Serbs. The laws which brought in new changes were not applied but all of the old laws in Croatia were applied as previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described this period of time as the time of great political tensions. 1991 was about to start. Was it a year that was marked by something peculiar that was happening in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, 1991 is the beginning of the war, although political tensions existed back in 1990, but the war began in 1991. This is the year when Slovenia first seceded, when the federal government sent its forces to Slovenia, to the border there, and when our soldiers were killed in great numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Can you find a link between Mr. Spegelj, who was a minister in the government of Croatia, and the events of January 1991?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned Mr. Spegelj earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, just before we get to Mr. Spegelj, I just want to understand what is meant by "our soldiers." You said: "This is the year when Slovenia first seceded, when the federal government sent its forces to is Slovenia, to the border there, and when our soldiers were killed in great numbers." Who are the "our"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm using a colloquial term. I said "ours." Up until that time the only regular soldiers were those of the Yugoslav People's Army, so they should have been soldiers of all of us living in the former Yugoslavia. They should have been also the soldiers of Slovenia, but this is not how people there perceived them unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So by "our," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely what I just said; namely, that no other regular army existed at the time except for the Yugoslav People's Army. At that time, I was a national of the federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia. The Yugoslav People's Army was the regular army of that state, so those soldiers were our soldiers or my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The Yugoslav People's Army, you mean the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Spegelj, who was the Minister of Defence in the government of Croatia. Is his name linked to the events in late 1990, 1991?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned him in the context of the political "salto mortale" that was committed by the Party for Democratic Changes. Mr. Spegelj appeared as a protagonist in a documentary during that period of time which was broadcast by the information service of the JNA, and the film depicted the process of arming. In addition to Mr. Spegelj, there appeared also Djuro Decak and Mr. Boljkovac, also high officials. Recently we heard that on the 30th or 31st of May, when Croatia celebrated their statehood, there was a programme broadcast on Croatian television and I watched it. In it they said that back in September 1990 they started arming themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say they were arming themselves in September of 1990. Who was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Croatia was establishing paramilitary formations, first through this irregular increase of employees of the Ministry of the Interior and later on through establishment of the so-called National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this also entail the creation of new units that were outside of the JNA, and did this lead to conflicts? Do you know of any conflicts in early 1991, armed conflicts, in the territory of the then Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The situation continued deteriorating. Conflicts and clashes erupted; I'm aware of the one in Pakrac, and in the spring there was one in Plitvice. I think it was on the 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt again? I'm sorry to do this to you, Mr. Milovancevic. A little earlier, Mr. Licina, you said: "Recently we heard that on the 30th or 31st of May, when Croatia celebrated their statehood, there was a programme broadcast on Croatian television and I watched it." 30th or 31st of May of which year? You said "recently." Now I'm not so worried -- May 2006 or which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to May of 2006. This was a programme on the occasion of their independence anniversary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I wanted to clarify this too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who participated in this programme and who spoke about the arming?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was Minister Spegelj, Minister Boljkovac. Mostly people from the then establishment, either ministers, Minister of Defence, Minister of the Interior and some of their military officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that now, in May of 2006, during a TV programme, they announced that back in September of 1990, they had started the process of arming in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. And this TV programme should be -- could be located in the archives of Croatian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a conflict in Plitvice which was rather close to your birth town. Who clashed there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The Plitvice Lakes is an area in Korenica municipality which is a neighbouring municipality to Gracac municipality. Croatian police forces made a raid in Plitvice. They were disguised as Italian tourists. Plitvice is a national park. It used to be one of the most beautiful national parks in the former Yugoslavia. So these police forces raided the area and a conflict erupted. Rajko Vukadinovic, who was a Serb, died in the clash, and Josip Jovic I think is the name of the Croat who died on their side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of any possible JNA intervention?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA intervened, they separated the two sides, and created a buffer area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That was in late March 1991. The month of May was marked by some events. Can you tell us what happened in Borovo Selo, Trogir, Zadar? Do you know of events in those towns? If not, just say so briefly.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I know what was generally made public. I know that there were attacks on barracks, and there were two important political events in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which events do you have in mind, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: There were two referendums. Croatia scheduled a referendum on the 16th of May, I believe, on secession from Yugoslavia, whereas on the 12th of May, the government of SAO Krajina scheduled a referendum on seceding from Croatia and remaining within Yugoslavia. Rather, first of all, it was defined as the annexation to Serbia and secession from Croatia. This is how the question was formulated at the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the results of these two referendums?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: In the territory of Krajina, once again, over 99 per cent, I believe, voted in favour, so the convincing, overwhelming majority. However, in the territory of Croatia they didn't vote. So the remaining population was, I don't know, 70 to 80 per cent, and within them, those who were Croats voted to secede from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The issue of remaining in Yugoslavia or seceding from Yugoslavia, was it the main political issue which first arose in 1989 and then continued on through those referendums?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. That was the essential question, the key to the crisis and to the war, because without that issue there would have been no war. The statement of Franjo Tudjman at the end of the war, I think in 1995, clearly illustrates this. It could have been 1995 or 1996. Tudjman said there would have been no war had Croatia not wanted one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the population in Croatia split. There were those who were Serbs, residents of Croatia, who were in favour of remaining within Yugoslavia, and then there were Croats who wanted independence and secession from Yugoslavia. Do you know whether, in accordance with the then constitution of Yugoslavia it was possible to decide on secession from Yugoslavia or remaining in Yugoslavia without other nations participating in that referendum?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: No. It wasn't possible under the then constitution. The decision on whether a republic would secede or not could only be taken by all republics together. This is how it was set forth in the constitution of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Slovenia and Croatia seek for this consent when they seceded?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Slovenia and Croatia never received such consent, so their secession was a violent act, a unilateral act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: His Honour Moloto asked you about the events in 1991 when you said "our" soldiers. So Croatia and Slovenia declared their secession in late June 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware with what was taking place in Slovenia immediately following this declaration of secession?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, I think that the federal government took the decision for the federal forces to take over border patrol and the border area. The units were sent to the border area. However, the forces of the JNA, to whom I colloquially referred as our soldiers, came under attack there and soldiers were killed. Since the soldiers were not given an order to shoot, this was basically an open season, to hunt the soldiers down. Following some time, the Presidency of the SFRY took the decision to withdraw the forces temporarily, as they termed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you said "to withdraw the forces temporarily," which forces were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was that in July of 1991; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. I can't put the date on it but I think it was the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened after that in Croatia? How did the situation evolve? We are now in August of 1991. What was the situation with the Serb people in Croatia and what was the status of the JNA in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The position of the Serb people was deteriorating. They were basically hunted down, especially in urban areas. So that a large number of people where Serbs were not a majority fled those areas. I think there is a report by Boutros Boutros-Ghali specifying that 251.000 refugees, Serbs, fled that area from the territory which was not part of Krajina. Simultaneously there were general attacks against the JNA barracks. Not general attacks but, rather, attacks in those towns where Croats had a significant majority. I remember a very illustrative example in Split, when Croatian extremists strangled a JNA soldier. I believe he was a Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the blockades, about how the barracks were blocked off and how electricity and water supply was cut off? When did the conflict, armed conflict erupt?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: It was in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That was a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, this witness has not told us anything about cutoff of electricity, and the objection is that you are leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw that part of my question about the cutting off of electrical, water and telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will ask the witness whether he knows anything about the armed conflict in the area of the then Socialist Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that and I've said so previously, that there were blockades. And what you just described is the same thing as the blockades. The blockades meant that the barracks had been cut off, as were electrical, water and telephone supply lines. So this is nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any armed operations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. The barracks came under attack. I remember the case, I think in Bjelovar, when Major Tepic was killed. I think that there were many similar examples. However, I only heard about this from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need to dwell further on this because your information comes only from the media. What was the situation like in your municipality of Gracac in 1991? What were you doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: At the time, the 9th Knin Corps was founded, and it mobilised everybody who was fit for military service. All of us at the time, mostly responded to the JNA call-up papers and went to the army. The order was issued to lift the siege of the barracks in the area of responsibility of the Knin Corps. At that time, our Gracac Brigade also was part of the Knin Corps. I think that it was called the 9th Brigade but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a follow-up question, let me ask you this: When giving your personal details, you said that you served your regular military service in the JNA, and I think you completed it in 1984.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you serve? In which branch of service?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: In the signals unit in Bjeline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the then Yugoslavia, up until 1991, did every male fit for military service have his military assignment within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. After completing our mandatory military service, all of us received our assignments, and then we had to go to exercises, manoeuvres, or received our wartime assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "all of us," who do you have in mind, Mr. Licina? Do you have in mind all males fit to serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I have in mind all military conscripts, everybody fit for military service in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was the rule at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the obligation to respond to a military call-up envisioned by law and was there any punishment for failure to respond?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Everyone was legally bound to respond to a military call-up and there were sanctions provided for those who failed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the autumn and winter of 1991, you were living in Gracac, as you say. You received a military call-up paper and to what unit did you report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, I reported to our unit, the Gracac Brigade of the territory of Gracac municipality. That's the unit I was assigned to, according to my military assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you mobilised into a regular JNA unit or a Territorial Defence unit?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: I was mobilised to a Territorial Defence unit which was part of the regular armed forces. All the units there were part of the Territorial Defence except for some few soldiers who were doing their obligatory military service. When referring to the Gracac brigade, I'm not referring to a brigade that arrived from elsewhere. These were all local people from Gracac who were military conscripts mobilised into that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Until when were you part of this Territorial Defence unit as a military conscript?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, practically until the arrival of UNPROFOR, when the Vance Plan was accepted and the UN forces were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, did you participate in any military operations and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. I participated in the operation to de-block the barracks in Sveti Rok. That's a place on the territory of our municipality. Our Gracac brigade was given the task of lifting the siege on the Sveti Rok barracks. Sveti Rok, or Saint Roko, in the Gracac municipality, is a place where there was a small military crew and a large military depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is page 25 of our atlas, square D2. Gracac is in the middle, a little to the right, and from there, there is a road leading to a place called Sveti Rok, and then Lovinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said there was an operation to lift the siege of the barracks. Does this mean there were JNA military facilities in Sveti Rok?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, as I said, in Sveti Rok, there was a small military unit and a large JNA depot. This was a depot where mines and explosives were stored for the Zagreb military district and for the Territorial Defence of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that as a member of the Territorial Defence you were mobilised and that an armed action was carried out to lift the siege. Who was laying siege to the barracks? What forces and where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The barracks was under siege and this was done by the forces I mentioned previously in my testimony. These were forces of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, or the National Guard Corps, established in Lovinac. These were the legal new forces established in the area of Lovinac and Sveti Rok and they were attacking the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this lifting of the siege took place, this military action you participated in?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: This took place in the second half of September nineteen --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the year. The interpreter heard 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you say what unit participated in this and whether there was a conflict and with whom and how it all ended?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a conflict. Previously in the area a policeman had been wounded. He came from the Gracac police station. I think his last name was Miljus. After that, two of our citizens from Gracac went missing, Rajko Dragosavac and Branko Veselinovic. After that, two days later, another citizen of ours was killed. His name was Srecko Kolundzic [phoen]. And then we attempted to lift the siege of the barracks and to destroy the military force laying siege to the barracks. There was fighting in which two of our fighters were killed on the first day. Djuro Cedlan [phoen] and Nikolai Ivanic [phoen] were the two fighters of ours who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Licina. I will interrupt you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the transcript it says that this was happening in September 1995. This must be a slip. It should be September 1991. If this could be put on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you said that in Lovinac and the surrounding area there were places of the Croatian government, of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior and National Guard Corps, and you mentioned four or five names of persons who were killed. What ethnicity were the people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: The people I mentioned, the one person who was wounded and the five who were killed were all ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that the fighting started. Can you tell us with whom you fought, what you attacked, whether there was any resistance. I don't want to put any leading questions.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, our forces were then attacking. We were starting from a Serbian village called Stikada. The next place is called Rucice. That's a passage between two mountains, Velebit and Dresnik, about two or four kilometres. That was the width of that pass. And our forces passed through that valley. The Croatian forces were deployed in the shape of a letter T. Rucice are in the foot-hills, and then there is Cerije [phoen], and then Sveti Rok and Lovinac are on two sides. In Sveti Rok, that's where the barracks is, our forces advanced from the direction of Gracac and, as I say, on the first day, those two men were killed, of ours, and later on during the night, the Croatian forces pulled out through Mount Velebit in the direction of Gospic, and left the area leaving it vacant. As far as I know, most of the population left together with the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is that how the barracks was de-blocked in Sveti Rok?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe what equipment and materiel was used -- was in those depots?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. As I said previously, the barracks in Sveti Rok were in fact a military depot. This was a depot where mines and explosives were stored, both for the Zagreb military district and for the Territorial Defence. It was the most important military warehouse in the area. The size of the depot is best illustrated by the fact that after the siege was lifted and we entered the barracks, our Gracac Brigade, which was there, spent seven or eight or even 10 days loading that materiel onto trucks. So this was taken to Bosnia and to Serbia. So this was a huge depot. You can imagine a company of some 50 people working in the warehouse all day, loading this and you can't see any result. That's how huge it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there only one such warehouse or more than one?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: There was more than one such warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the mines and explosives intended for the army were taken to Bosnia and Serbia, were they transported for the republics of Bosnia and Croatia or did the JNA do this for itself?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Well, of course, the JNA transported this to its warehouses elsewhere, according to their own deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the events in Lovinac, we have heard other explanations. We have heard that the aim of the attack on Lovinac was to expel the entire Croatian population in order to create an ethnic space for the Serbs. Does this fit into the information you are giving us?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: No. This is not correct. The Croatian population did leave, it's true, together with those forces. But as far as I know, they had no losses there. Some elderly people even remained in Lovinac. I remember some of those people very well. And in contacts with the Red Cross and their families, we took those people to be reunited with their families. There was a slightly comical situation where some people who remained, who remained among us all that time, there was a man by the name of Ante Pavelic among them. Ante Pavelic was the leader of the independent state of Croatia in World War II. He was a notorious person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from what happened in Lovinac, where there was a JNA warehouse, do you know of any similar cases where new Croatian police stations were established?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: As I said, this happened in every municipality where the Serbs were in the majority, but where there were some villages where there was a Croatian minority within that municipality. I don't want this to sound pejorative. I'm simply referring to numbers. This situation obtained in Lovinac, for Gracac municipality, in Kijevo for Knin municipality, in Krusevo for Obrovac municipality, in Skabrnja, I think for Benkovac municipality, in Vidusevac for Glina municipality, and so on. You could find such cases everywhere. And this was actually what generated the crisis in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the attack on the JNA barracks in Sveti Rok, do you know of anything about attacks on JNA barracks in Dalmatia along the coast?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes. As I said earlier, there was a case in Split, an incident in Split that I remember. And along the Adriatic coast, I think there were similar incidents in Zadar and that the forces of the Knin Corps set out in order to lift the siege in Zadar. I think the brigade commander was -- I can't recall his name. Oh, yes, Slavko Lisica. I remember it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were one of the founders and members of the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the aims of that party, the political aspirations and intentions. Can you tell us whether, in this period we are referring to, August to December 1995 -- 1991, at any meeting where you participated, was there any discussion about expelling the Croatian population, creating conditions which would force the Croatian population to leave, killing, persecuting and so on?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA
utterances.text: This was never the goal of the SDS and its leadership. As I said previously, the Serb Democratic Party had among its members other ethnicities, even Croats, and what I say can be supported by the fact that there were some soldiers in the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, who were killed. For example, in the Medak pocket action, Jure Ivasic [phoen], an honourable Croat from Gracac, was killed. He remained with us all the time and was in our army. Also recently, this year, there was an exhumation, and news reached us that victims of Operation Storm had been exhumed, one of which was Dr. Drazan Koritnik. He was a doctor in Donji Lapac. He was an ethnic Croat but he lived with us throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think this may be a good time for breaking for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The matter is now adjourned to tomorrow. I think it's at 9.00 in the morning. The matter stands adjourned to 9.00 tomorrow morning in this court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
